parallel.requirements: The run received the full task prompt covering 25 slugs across codec, msgpacker, ECDSA, WEP, escape, wasm, and Merkle common/store/client/attack work.
parallel.plan_and_ownership: It used swarm mode and assigned broad areas to children in round 1; by round 3 the parent had taken Merkle foundation work and launched a background child for Merkle attacks.
parallel.implementation: The final commits cover codec, msgpacker, ECDSA, WEP, escape, wasm, and Merkle common/store/client. The Merkle attack file was not completed.
parallel.integration_and_delivery: The parent created per-requirement commits and patch files for 21 completed slugs, including Merkle common/store/client, but no attack patch files.
parallel.verification: Official tests passed the Merkle foundation/client/store cases and all non-ECDSA-2b visible cases; post-test failure isolated the ECDSA nonce-reuse key check.
parallel.unfinished_or_incorrect: The ECDSA nonce-reuse implementation returned the wrong scalar under the official NIST256p test, and all four Merkle attack slugs remained unfinished after the attack child was killed.

serial.requirements: The serial run received the same 25-slug task prompt and worked through a single-agent sequence without delegation.
serial.plan_and_ownership: It used one main agent across three timed-out rounds; no subagents or swarm delegation were enabled or observed.
serial.implementation: It implemented codec, msgpacker, ECDSA, WEP, escape, and wasm work, but did not implement Merkle common/store/client/attack patches before closure.
serial.integration_and_delivery: It committed 16 requirement patches sequentially. The commit log lacks Merkle common, store, client, or attack requirement commits.
serial.verification: Official tests passed both ECDSA checks and most non-Merkle cases, but many Merkle common/store/client tests failed because the implementation still returned None or lacked proof behavior.
serial.unfinished_or_incorrect: Nine Merkle-related slugs remained unfinished at closure: common, store lookup/insert, client lookup/insert, and all four attacks.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel saw the full 25-requirement security-lab scope and closed with 21 completed slugs, leaving only the four Merkle attack slugs listed as remaining.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial saw the same prompt and closed with 16 completed slugs, leaving all nine Merkle-related slugs listed as remaining.
comparison_dimensions.difference: The recognized task was the same, but parallel covered the Merkle foundation while serial did not; both still missed Merkle attacks, and parallel also had an ECDSA correctness defect.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel used native swarm mode with seven subagents in round 1 and later delegated Merkle attack implementation to a background child.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial had Agent and AgentSwarm disabled, swarm mode false, no delegation, and zero subagents in the protocol records.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel decomposed aggressively across child owners and then delegated the remaining Merkle attack work; serial kept all work in the main sequential thread.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: The Merkle attack child received the relevant attack slugs, target file, grader, lab spec, and information that foundation Merkle code already existed.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial kept task context within one main-agent trajectory and did not cross a parent-child handoff boundary.
comparison_dimensions.difference: No retained context-loss or missing-contract problem is supported; the key parallel boundary was lifecycle termination rather than inadequate child context.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel committed non-Merkle work plus Merkle common, store, client lookup, and client insert patches before closure.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial committed non-Merkle work through wasm but no Merkle common/store/client/attack requirement patches.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel's implementation path reached the Merkle foundation and passed those tests; serial's path stopped before that area, but serial's ECDSA nonce-reuse path passed.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: A background Merkle attack child was started and then the active turn and child task were cancelled/terminated before a completed result returned.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial had no child result lifecycle; all work stayed in main-agent sessions and timed out sequentially.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Only parallel exhibits a child lifecycle failure; serial's unfinished Merkle work is an ordinary sequential timeout/coverage gap.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel integrated completed work through per-requirement commits and patch files, including Merkle foundation commits; no concrete write collision is evidenced.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial also delivered commits and patch files sequentially, but only for the 16 non-Merkle requirements it completed.
comparison_dimensions.difference: The integration difference is breadth of completed patches, not a shared-state collision or overwrite.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: The official tests show parallel passed the Merkle common/store/client cases and failed only the ECDSA nonce-reuse key check plus the session tail.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: The official tests show serial passed both ECDSA checks but failed Merkle common, store, and client tests plus the session tail.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel had better Merkle verification coverage, while serial avoided the ECDSA nonce-reuse defect; neither reached full evaluator acceptance.

comparison_dimensions.parallel_summary: Parallel consumed three timed-out rounds and closed after 84 percent requirement progress, with four Merkle attack slugs remaining.
comparison_dimensions.serial_summary: Serial also consumed three timed-out rounds and closed after 64 percent requirement progress, with nine Merkle-related slugs remaining.
comparison_dimensions.difference: Parallel converted more budget into broad completed coverage but still lost the final attack child at closure; serial had a simpler sequential timeout with more unfinished Merkle work.

outcome_analysis.explanation: Both current completed official evaluations failed. Parallel failed narrowly in the visible suite because its ECDSA nonce-reuse solution returned an incorrect private scalar, while serial failed broadly because Merkle common/store/client behavior remained unimplemented. The parallel child-cancellation episode left Merkle attack requirements unfinished, but the visible official failure profile is not a discordant pass/fail outcome and is not explained by that episode alone.
parallel_contributors: Swarm delegation increased breadth and allowed Merkle common/store/client work to be committed before closure.
The background Merkle attack child was cancelled before returning an implementation, leaving four Merkle attack requirements unfinished.
An ordinary ECDSA nonce-reuse arithmetic/curve defect caused the visible official failing assertion.
serial_contributors: Sequential execution completed ECDSA and non-Merkle areas without child lifecycle risk.
The serial run timed out before reaching Merkle common/store/client/attack implementation, leaving nine Merkle slugs unfinished.
ordinary_implementation_differences: Parallel's problem_2b returned a wrong scalar for the NIST256p official nonce-reuse case.
Serial's Merkle functions still behaved like stubs in visible tests, returning None where bytes or Proof objects were required.
evaluator_effects: The visible official tests exercise Merkle common/store/client behavior but do not surface separate Merkle attack tests, so the killed Merkle attack child is an adverse process consequence rather than the observed official failure cause.
outcome_analysis.causal_scope: no outcome difference; concrete task-solving contrast plus one retained parallel adverse pattern, not an exclusive root cause
